opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think of them a bit like sentinels. The liver in particular sits at this crossroads of the body: everything you absorb from the gut passes through it via the portal circulation, it's doing an enormous amount of metabolic work, and it filters drugs and toxins. So when something systemic is going on, whether that's chemotherapy, inflammation, a metabolic shift, or the spread of a tumor, the liver often shows it, sometimes before anything is obvious anywhere else.

The spleen is similar in a different way. It's part of the immune system and it filters the blood, so it reacts to infection, to immune activation, and to changes in blood cell turnover. It can enlarge, or its texture can change, in response to things happening far away from it.

What's interesting from an imaging and machine learning standpoint is that we scan these organs all the time, usually incidentally. Someone gets a CT for their colorectal cancer, for example, and the liver and spleen are right there in the image. Historically a radiologist looks for obvious things, like a metastasis or a clearly enlarged spleen, and otherwise the organs are called normal. But there's a lot of subtle information in the texture and the intensity patterns that the human eye isn't really trained to quantify. With radiomics and deep learning we can start to pull out those signals and ask whether the liver is telling us something about how a patient will respond to treatment, whether they're developing toxicity from chemotherapy, or whether disease is likely to recur.

So I see the liver and spleen less as just organs we check off and more as windows into the whole patient's physiology. If we can learn to read them quantitatively, we get that information essentially for free from scans patients are already getting.

r001.rationale: The response says the spleen reacts to infection, immune activation, and blood-cell turnover, and that it can change in response to events happening elsewhere in the body.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it is that the liver and spleen are these incredibly honest organs. They don't really hide anything. Almost everything that happens in the body passes through the liver at some point, and the spleen is sitting right there in the immune and blood systems, so when something is going wrong elsewhere, these two organs tend to respond. They change size, they change texture, they change how they take up contrast on a scan, long before a patient necessarily feels anything.

A lot of my work has been on CT imaging in cancer patients, and what struck me early on is how much information in those scans just gets thrown away. A radiologist is looking for the tumor, which is the right thing to do clinically, but the scan has also captured the liver, the spleen, the muscle, the fat. If you measure those systematically, you start to see patterns. Spleen volume, for instance, can go up when there's portal hypertension or when the liver is under stress from chemotherapy. Liver texture changes with steatosis, with fibrosis, with treatment toxicity. And those changes end up correlating with things we actually care about, like whether a patient tolerates surgery, how they respond to therapy, how long they survive.

So I tend to think of them as readouts. The cancer is the primary problem, but the body's response to the cancer, and to the treatment, is written in these organs. And because they're imaged over and over in routine care, we have longitudinal data essentially for free. Computationally, that's a gift. We can segment them automatically now, extract quantitative features, and track trajectories across time rather than relying on a single snapshot or a qualitative impression like "the spleen looks a bit enlarged."

The thing I always try to emphasize is that none of this replaces the clinician. It's about surfacing signals that are already in the image but that no human has time to quantify by hand across thousands of patients. The liver and spleen are telling us something. We just haven't been listening very carefully.

r001.rationale: The response says the spleen tends to respond when something is going wrong elsewhere in the body, presenting it as a readout of the body's condition.

astra-6.text:
I think of the liver and spleen as windows into what’s happening throughout the body. The liver is involved in metabolism and processing what circulates in our blood, while the spleen is closely involved in immune function. So changes in those organs can reflect more than a problem in the organs themselves; they may tell us something about a person’s broader health.

From an imaging perspective, that’s an interesting opportunity. Can we measure changes in their size or appearance and use those as clues to what’s happening elsewhere? The challenge is that those changes aren’t necessarily specific to one condition. We have to interpret them alongside the rest of the clinical picture.

r001.rationale: It describes the spleen as a window into what is happening throughout the body and says changes in it can reflect broader health.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the liver and spleen as windows into what’s happening throughout the body. The liver processes nutrients, medications, and many of the substances circulating in our blood, so changes there can reflect broader metabolic health. The spleen is closely involved in immune function and filtering the blood, so it gives us a different, complementary view.

What interests me is whether we can pick up those signals in medical images. We routinely look at an image to answer a specific question, but there may be information in the size, shape, or texture of these organs that tells us something about a person’s overall health. The challenge is connecting those imaging patterns to meaningful biological changes, so we can understand what they’re actually telling us.

r001.rationale: The response says the spleen’s immune and blood-filtering functions provide a complementary view of overall health, framing it as a source of signals about the body beyond the spleen itself.
